thread.title: Retirement: Should You Prepare For The Next Downturn Now?

author: Financially Free Investor
title: Retirement: Should You Prepare For The Next Downturn Now?
text:
We are not trying to sound an alarm. In fact, the markets are just doing fine. Even though the volatility is a bit high and there are worries over trade and tariffs, rising interest rates and host of other issues, but the markets may eventually climb over the wall of worry and continue to touch new highs. Moreover, we have no ability to predict the short-term or even mid-term direction of the markets. We do not know when the next downturn or recession will arrive; it may, in fact, be a few years away. Then why are we writing on this topic? Well, the first thing we can do is not to worry about day-to-day market gyrations. Secondly, the right time to prepare for a downturn is when things are going relatively well.
A Case In Support Of A Bear Market: Consider the following facts that we already know:
The current bull market is in its 10 th year and the second longest in history. At this rate, provided it continues, it is going to be ‘the longest’ in history in a few months since the previous longest bull market lasted for 114 months from Oct. 1990 to Mar. 2000. The current P/E of the broader market as represented by S&P500 was 24.09 as of 06/01/2018, even though the estimated forward P/E is only about 17.15. However, forward P/E is not a reliable metric, because it assumes that the current economic expansion will continue for the foreseeable future. The yearly average of P/E since 1871 is just about 15.70. The Shiller PE ratio at the end of the March 2018 stood at 31.30, which is highest in the history except for two instances, one during the dotcom bubble and another in September of 1929, just before the great depression. Note: The Shiller Price to Earnings ratio is based on average inflation-adjusted earnings from the previous ten years, known as the Cyclically Adjusted PE Ratio or CAPE).
Chart courtesy Quandl.com .
The Federal Reserve has been raising the short-term rates in its pursuit to normalize the rates. It has made its intention clear to continue raising the interest rates in 2018 and 2019. Even though the rates have been rising slowly, and there is always a chance that the Feds could alter their stance when faced with new information. At the same time, there is a chance that the Fed may go too far and in turn, actually causes the next economic downturn and recession. Last but not the least, let’s not forget the geopolitical risks and trade tensions, which remain on the horizon. However, this is of our least concern. A Case In Support Of A Continuing Bull Market: Nonetheless, there is a case for the bull market to continue as well. The bull market may continue for another couple of years:
It is often said that the bull markets don’t die of old age. The current bull market may be getting old, but usually, the maximum amount of gains are accrued in the final stage of the bull market. For example, by 1997, the S&P500 was up by 33%, but it continued to gain another 50% in its final two years. Below is a chart of showing growth of S&P500 between 1990-2003 (in Red) and overlapped by the current bull-period 2009-2018 (in Blue).
Chart by Author
However, we do not know if the current stage will prove to be like the year 1997 or 2000. But we haven’t had a parabolic move this time, which happened last time from 1997-1999 before the crash. Though this chart can be interpreted for either a bull or a bear scenario, depending upon who is looking at it, but we think the current bull may still run for some more time. There are tailwinds as well such as the corporate tax-reform signed by President Trump. So many of the corporations will be taking advantage of lower taxes, and this makes more cash available for investments in business and of course share-buybacks and dividend raises. Also, let’s not forget the hundreds of millions of dollars parked overseas by big corporations, some of which is being (or can be) repatriated at lower taxes. Even if the majority of cash is used to share-buybacks, though it may not do much to boost the economy, it will still provide a boost to the share prices. The US economy has been expanding since the great recession, but the Euro economy started growing only since 2013. It was only last year that all of the major economies of the world had positive growth for the first time since the financial crisis. According to World Bank, the global economy is likely to continue expanding at the current pace until 2020. Of course, this could be interrupted by any of the hot-button issues getting out-of-control for example, trade-frictions, oil-prices getting too expansive or some geopolitical issues like North Korea. Obviously, the battle between the bulls and bears will continue. We cannot possibly solve that puzzle. As investors, while we should keep a tab on the overall environment and shape of the economy, we have no control over most of them. However, what we can do is to be prepared for good times as well as bad. We always hope for the best, but we need to be prepared for any of the negative scenarios.
How To Analyze The Risks In Your Portfolio? Keeping all your money in CASH would make no sense just in anticipation of a market downturn or recession. Similarly, it probably makes no sense to keep all your money in stocks or stock indexes while most of them are very close to their peaks. We certainly need a middle approach. However, what you do is mostly dependent upon your personal situation as well. The factors like the time-horizon in the market, size of the investment pool, income needs, risk-tolerance, etc. should guide your actions.
Let’s consider a generalized scenario. In the current market environment, while we want to capture some of the gains (if not all) from the bullish market, we still want to protect our downside. We normally like to do an exercise as presented below to judge if we have the risk-appetite for the portfolio that we have or if we need to make adjustments.

So, what is the purpose of this exercise? By doing this, we get to know the worst outcome for our portfolio in a bad situation. If this was something that we could not tolerate for a day and much more than our risk-appetite, we must adjust the portfolio accordingly. And the time to adjust the portfolio to suit your risk-appetite is now when the markets are still doing just fine. If your portfolio is not organized in a fashion that you can determine the risk, maybe it’s time to work on it.
How And Why To Prepare Now: It is better to prepare and make your portfolio risk-averse or should we say risk-appropriate now, when the markets are still doing fine. You do not have to take any decisions under panic or distress because markets are still doing okay. We may or may not get this luxury at some point in the future, how distant it may be.
We like to suggest to divide your overall portfolio into multiple buckets, each having distinct goals and risk-levels. Also, care should be taken that each bucket has a different correlation to the broader stock-market, so as when one zigs, the other one may zag.
Note: According to Investopedia , stock-market correlation is defined as a statistic that measures the degree to which any two securities move in relation to each other. Correlation is computed into what is known as the correlation coefficient , which has a value that must fall between -1 and 1. For example, if two securities move exactly in the same fashion, then the correlation will be a perfect 1.
We will describe one such portfolio of three buckets. We will try to keep things simple, though it will definitely be more complex than investing in S&P500 or a bunch of ETFs. You could read our article on a portfolio of ETFs here .
Here are the three simple goals for the overall portfolio:
Capture at least 70-80% of the gains of the broader market, in bullish times. The maximum drawdown should not exceed 50-60% of the drawdown of the broader market. For example, the market drops 50%, portfolio drops only 25-30%. Provide 5% income in good times and bad. To keep the above goals in mind, we will suggest a portfolio of three buckets for moderately conservative investors:
DGI portfolio (40%):
20-25 stocks, at least half of them trading at 15%- 25% below their 52-week high Earn an average income of 4% Maximum drawdown of 70% of S&P500. INCOME portfolio (35%):
Roughly 8% income on an average. Correlation of less than 0.60 with S&P500 Diversified into different types of assets. Risk-averse Bonds & Treasury Portfolio (25%)
Earn an average income of 4% Consists of Bonds, Treasuries, and Inflation-protected Treasuries. Correlation with the broader market of less than 0.25. For very conservative investors (or folks who cannot stand big drawdowns), we would eliminate the high-income bucket and divide the entire amount in just DGI (65%) and Bonds/Treasury (35%). However, they will need to tamp down their income expectations to about 4%.
Bucket 1: DGI Strategy Type – Active Passive 15-20 stocks, half of them trading at least 15%- 25% below their 52-week high Earn an average income of 4% Maximum drawdown of 70% of S&P500. We will select 20 stocks in this bucket. At least half of them will be selected based on valuation. We ran a screener to find out companies that are large, blue-chip but trading at least 12-25% below their 52-week high. Though we got more than 50 companies based on our criteria, we selected a few companies that we thought are cheap due to some adverse environment, but they are still solid blue-chip companies with long history of paying dividends. For more details of the screener and the criteria for cheap DGI stocks, please see one of our previous articles . The criteria are also described below in brief. Please note that some of the companies on our list did not satisfy all the criteria but we added them for sector diversification. Examples are AAPL, MSFT, XOM, UL, and DWX.

Bucket 2: High Income (REITs, CEFs, BDCs) Strategy Type – Semi-Active Roughly 8% average income. Correlation of less than 0.60 with S&P500 Diversified into different types of assets. This basket will consist of high-income securities, mainly REITs, mREITs, BDCs and some CEFs. Its main purpose is to generate high income, preferably 8%. This will help compensate a lower level of income from other baskets, and thus reduce the need to take risks in other baskets. In that sense, this is also the riskiest basket within our portfolio. However, it is very well-diversified and will invest in different types of assets like REITs, BDCs ( Business Development Companies), and CEFs ( Closed-End Funds), and we believe it probably has no more risk than the broader market.

The total income on a $350,000 portfolio would be $27,160. The correlation factor of this portfolio with the broader market is less than 0.55.
Bucket 3: Bonds/Treasuries Strategy Type – Passive Earn an average income of 3% plus. Consists of Bonds, Treasuries, and Inflation-protected Treasuries. Correlation of less than 0.25 with the broader market to balance the volatility in other portfolios We will invest this bucket in four securities (ETFs). The overall correlation with the broader market is only 0.21. We selected the below four funds for the reasons like low expense ratio, broad diversification, and the reasonable yield. However, the investors could replace them with other funds of their choice as long as they belong to the similar asset class. Besides, we allocate 10% (within this basket) to a Gold fund, which provides no income but should provide the hedge against inflation and the US Dollar.
Bond Fund: For Bond allocation, we will invest 35% of this bucket in iShares Core U.S. Aggregate Bond ETF ( AGG ).This fund tracks an index of US investment-grade bonds. The market-weighted index includes Treasuries, agencies, MBS, CMBS, and investment-grade corporate bonds. The fund has a very low expense ratio of 0.05% compared to its peers. It currently provides a decent yield in the range of 2.80%.
Inflation-Protected Treasuries: We will allocate 35% of the capital of this bucket to the iShares TIPS Bond ETF (NYSEARCA: TIP ), which seeks to match the Bloomberg Barclays U.S. Treasury Inflation Protected Securities ( OTC:TIPS ) Index (composed of inflation-protected U.S. Treasury bonds). The fund has a weighted average maturity of about 8 years.
Preferred Stocks: We will allocate 20% to the Nuveen Preferred & Income Opportunities Fund (NYSE: JPC ). This closed-end fund has a consistently good record and, by using some leverage, is able to provide 7.76% yield.
GOLD ETF : We will allocate 10% of this bucket in a Gold ETF like IAU. This will provide a hedge against inflation as well as some kind of crisis or panic situations. The drawback, of course, would be that gold ETFs provide no income.

Conclusion: As you can see from above, we would get roughly 5.2% yield on the total portfolio. The overall yield is very respectable, though not very high. If you were to add social security income, we would be talking of $80,000 to $90,000 annual income for an average retired couple. Please remember that 65% of the portfolio is invested in highly conservative securities including 25% in bond-like securities. The DGI part of the portfolio is invested in proven blue-chip companies which have a long history of paying and raising dividends.
For a second, let’s assume that we are about to enter the next recession. Would we panic with this kind of portfolio? We think not. Mainly because the knowledge that we are invested in solid blue-chip companies, and we would still be getting high income. The average drawdown would be no more than 2/3 rd of the broader market. Even if a handful of the companies cut their distributions by 10-20%, sure that will be a temporary setback, but no reason to panic because of the fact that our investments would come roaring back once the recession clouds clear up.
But, let’s be optimistic, primarily because the economy is still on a solid footing in spite of all the worries. In either case, whether you feel optimistic or pessimistic about the market direction, this highly diversified, income producing portfolio will stand on its own in good times and bad.
